Logic isn’t just rules, it is creative. Our next two BIG Scholar profiles show how curiosity, persistence, and imagination shape the way students learn and build. For Gabriel Najmias 🇨🇷 #CostaRica , logic has always been a way to understand the world. As a child, he loved chess and card games that rewarded strategy and patience. Those same habits later led him to math Olympiads and computer science. He is a 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟯 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗢𝗹𝘆𝗺𝗽𝗶𝗮𝗱 𝗺𝗲𝗱𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝘁𝘂𝗱𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗦𝗰𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 University of Cambridge . His interests include machine learning, cybersecurity, and exploring how computing connects logic with real-world systems. Gabriel sees coding as a way to apply reasoning beyond theory. Whether debugging a program or setting trail cameras to film local wildlife, he approaches every challenge with the same curiosity and focus. 💭 His advice for young mathematicians considering Olympiads (as someone who came competitive math later than many of his peers): “Even though you might be a bit scared, and it might seem like the others are geniuses, you should always try. Give it a shot. Trust yourself.”

I am very excited to share that I obtained First Class Honours in my first year of Computer Science Tripos at the University of Cambridge , ranking 25/131 and 1st place in Object-Oriented Programming!

I got 10 new records in packing problems (2 had been held since 2007)! My approach: - Rank cells by how far each value sits above its predecessor compared to the table's usual step (big step → opportunity to find improvement). - Reconstruct current records from their image, freeze which edges/vertices touch which, converge that exactly, then apply noise and repeat. - Seed neighbouring cells from improved ones. Link to the code and writeup is here: https://lnkd.in/e25Rt7c5

Wrapping up an incredible 10 weeks working in Data at Bloomberg on the Company Financials Consumer team! This summer, I had the opportunity to work at the intersection of finance, data, and AI, while developing my skills in agentic solutions, machine learning, large scale databases, SQL, Python, and the Bloomberg Terminal. One of the highlights of my internship was designing and building an end to end agentic solution that worked across millions of financial data points and automated workflows that would have otherwise required more than 200 hours of manual work. More than anything, I’m grateful for how much I learned about both finance and technology, and for the opportunity to build something that had a real and quantified impact. A huge thank you to Cheick Sissoko and Adam Byrdak for their mentorship and guidance throughout the summer. The cherry on top: getting the chance to meet the person that revolutionized financial markets, Mike Bloomberg ! Grateful for an amazing summer and excited for what’s next!

That needs real thought on what talent and operating model is needed, getting the right data and tools in place to drive trustworthy recommendations, and change management throughout. A few recent life updates! Wrapped up my second year of CS at Cambridge and looking forward to heading into my third in October. I’ll be writing my dissertation on inverse protein folding models. I'm spending this summer at Briefcase . It's been a blast. I shipped my first end-to-end feature, mileage claims, and am now working on improving the autopublish rates. Thanks to Ján Stehlík and Reuben Steenkamp for the opportunity and Akash Bajwa for the intro! I’ve been working on a ton of projects on the side. A few recent ones: - Mind: A plug-and-play memory backend for AI agents which models the human brain. - Patience: A TypeScript framework for building queue-based AI agents. - Pinky: AI menu bar companion that watches your screen, learns your workflows and has a pointer that it can use to teach. - Loogle: my new personal website over at leostrijbos.com . Check it out. I’m currently working on batching and parallelisation infra for protein folding models. Feel free to reach out if this is something you are interested in or have some thoughts on.

Change is hard. Many large-scale transformations start with high energy, a clear plan, and the famous “quick wins” get executed. Thereafter, when the novelty wears off, exogenous volatility hits, and fatigue sets in, it’s tempting to quietly walk back on the ambition, push a few things into next year, and be happy with “good enough”. After analysing 72 companies with relevant experiences and data, the most successful organisations had a common factor of a culture that prioritised rigour, embodying speed, resilience, and consistency. It’s important to note that rigour does not imply rigidity. Disciplined execution in service of outcomes, adapting to market dynamics and operational challenges, becomes part of the way of working for top-quartile performers.
